articles.title: Como um casamento real na Alemanha deu origem à Oktoberfest | G1
articles.standfirst: A Oktoberfest nasceu para criar uma identidade germânica décadas antes de a Alemanha existir. Festa sobreviveu a duas guerras, se reinventou e se multiplicou.
articles.summary: A Oktoberfest nasceu para criar uma identidade germânica décadas antes de a Alemanha existir. Festa sobreviveu a duas guerras, se reinventou e se multiplicou.
articles.body:
Cerca de 6,5 milhões de visitantes compareceram à Oktoberfest de 2025 ao longo dos 16 dias de duração do evento. — Foto: Getty Images via BBC

Todos os anos, desde 1950, no primeiro sábado depois de 15 de setembro, o prefeito de Munique , a capital da Baviera, na Alemanha , tem um compromisso marcado.

Exatamente ao meio-dia, ele precisa estar na Theresienwiese (Campo de Teresa), uma grande área aberta perto do centro da cidade, em uma tenda, diante de um barril de cerveja e com um pesado martelo de madeira nas mãos.

Sua missão é introduzir uma torneira de latão, com a menor quantidade possível de golpes para evitar que a cerveja espirre.

Quando consegue, grita " O'zapft is! " (Já está aberta!), e exclama " Auf eine friedliche Wiesn! " (Por uma Oktoberfest em paz!), dando início ao disparo de 12 salvas de canhão a partir da escadaria da monumental estátua da Baviera, a mulher que simboliza a força, o orgulho e a identidade da região.

O som dos disparos de canhão é o tiro de largada do maior festival folclórico do mundo. Mais de seis milhões de pessoas chegam de todos os cantos do planeta para celebrar as tradições bávaras.

Muitos dos presentes, moradores ou não, usam os trajes típicos daquela região alpina.

Os homens usam lederhosen , calças curtas de couro, decoradas com bordados e presas por suspensórios; as mulheres usam dirndls , uma blusa branca, um corpete justo e um avental cujo laço revela sua situação amorosa: amarrado à esquerda significa que é solteira, e à direita, que o coração já está ocupado.

Durante os 16 ou 18 dias de duração do evento, a Theresienwiese se transforma em um gigantesco parque de diversões, com carrosséis e montanhas-russas.

Mas a verdadeira atração são seis enormes tendas. Nelas, são servidos rios de cerveja, uma quantidade suficiente para encher quase 3 piscinas olímpicas , frequentemente acompanhada por um dos mais de 1,2 milhão de brezn , enormes pretzels bávaros assados durante o festival.

Tudo é grande, abundante, barulhento e alegre, e tudo começou há mais de dois séculos , com outra festa popular exuberante, embora diferente, que não aconteceu em setembro nem, estritamente falando, na Alemanha , pois ainda faltavam seis décadas para que ela existisse como país.

Até Kim Kardashian visitou a Oktoberfest em 2010, quando usou um dirndl. — Foto: Getty Images via BBC

Em 1809, a inteligente e bela princesa Teresa de Saxe-Hildburghausen figurava na lista de candidatas a esposa de Napoleão Bonaparte, que procurava uma mulher de sangue real.

Quase toda a Europa estava sob o controle ou a influência do imperador francês. A Alemanha não existia como um país unificado; era um mosaico de pequenos reinos e ducados.

Luís, o príncipe herdeiro do recém-proclamado reino da Baviera, sentia uma rejeição visceral à imposição cultural e militar francesa e era um dos grandes promotores do incipiente nacionalismo cultural germânico: o sonho de uma identidade compartilhada para além das fronteiras.

Assim, viajou para conhecer Teresa e pediu sua mão quase imediatamente: uma união com uma princesa de um ducado germânico, em plena guerra napoleônica, era uma jogada de mestre.

"Eu me caso sem paixão, já que isso é mais vantajoso para o futuro", escreveu à sua irmã, a princesa Carolina Augusta da Baviera.

A falta de amor não era incomum nos casamentos reais. O insólito foi a forma como o casamento foi celebrado.

Em vez de uma cerimônia a portas fechadas com a aristocracia, convidaram o povo para uma festa descomunal de 5 dias, com a cidade iluminada, ópera e baile gratuitos, mesas com comida e cerveja custeadas pelo rei em praças e tavernas.

Houve até desfiles infantis com trajes típicos de regiões recém-anexadas ao reino, como a Francônia e a Suábia, pois a coroa bávara queria mais do que uma festa.

Segundo vários historiadores, a celebração foi planejada para que comunidades culturalmente distintas se percebessem como uma única nação.

A celebração culminou em 17 de outubro com uma corrida de cavalos em um campo fora das muralhas da cidade, à qual compareceram cerca de 40 mil pessoas.

Não parece muito em comparação com os milhões que chegam hoje ao mesmo local, até que se leva em conta que, segundo o Serviço de Estatística da Cidade de Munique , em 1810 a cidade tinha apenas 40.638 habitantes.

O sucesso foi tamanho que o rei decidiu batizar aquele campo em homenagem à sua nora. O local passou a se chamar Theresienwiese. E a festa, realizada originalmente em outubro, ficou conhecida como Oktoberfest.

Apresentação de cavalos e gado na primeira edição da Oktoberfest, uma celebração muito diferente da atual. — Foto: Getty Images via BBC

Quando a festa foi repetida no ano seguinte, houve uma exposição agrícola, algo que continua sendo feito hoje a cada três anos; as primeiras barracas de cerveja e o primeiro carrossel chegaram em 1818.

E, em 1872, depois de ouvir reclamações sobre o clima, as autoridades decidiram realizar o festival em setembro em vez de outubro, quando os dias são mais curtos, chuvosos e as temperaturas, menos agradáveis.

Mas pouco mais de um século depois daquele casamento, em 1914, a festa seria suspensa; quatro anos depois, a monarquia bávara deixaria de existir.

Durante os quatro anos que durou a Primeira Guerra Mundial, a Oktoberfest foi completamente cancelada. Não havia suprimentos, nem cevada para maltagem, nem ânimo para festas. O e ficou vazio de atrações.

A essa altura, a Alemanha como Estado-nação moderno já havia sido fundada. Foi em 1871, como uma monarquia constitucional e imperial governada por um Kaiser (o rei da Prússia).

Mas, em 1918, justamente quando a guerra terminava, a monarquia caiu. O último rei, Luís III da Baviera, fugiu, e o reino se transformou em uma república.

A vontade de reviver a Oktoberfest persistiu, mas o país estava mergulhado em uma profunda crise do pós-guerra que obrigou a organizar uma versão reduzida chamada Kleineres Herbstfest (Pequena Festa de Outono), até 1921, quando o nome original foi retomado e as grandes tendas, a música de sopros e a cerveja voltaram à Theresienwiese.

Com exceção de 1923, quando a pior crise de hiperinflação já sofrida pelo país obrigou ao cancelamento da festa, a tradição continuou alegremente, até Adolf Hitler chegar ao poder em 1933.

Naquele mesmo ano, foi proibido que judeus trabalhassem no festival. Cinco anos mais tarde, após a anexação da Áustria e dos Sudetos, o regime rebatizou o festival como " Großdeutsches Volksfest " — a festa popular da Grande Alemanha — e o utilizou como vitrine de uma identidade étnica que excluía ativamente aqueles que não se encaixavam nela.

A cerveja e o folclore, que um século antes haviam servido para unir os bávaros diante de um invasor estrangeiro, agora serviam para traçar uma linha entre aqueles que pertenciam à nação e os que não pertenciam.

Com a eclosão da Segunda Guerra Mundial, o festival foi suspenso. Não houve Oktoberfest entre 1939 e 1945.

A associação de Munique com o nazismo era difícil de apagar. — Foto: Getty Images via BBC

Quando a guerra terminou, Munique era uma cidade em ruínas que carregava o estigma de ter sido a "capital do movimento" nazista, e a Baviera, um território ocupado.

Como havia acontecido depois da Grande Guerra, durante três anos cinzentos, o festival sobreviveu com dificuldade como a Feira de Outono, que ocupava apenas um terço do espaço habitual da Theresienwiese e estava sujeita a severas restrições.

A tradicional cerveja de alto teor alcoólico da Oktoberfest estava proibida, porque o governo militar americano permitia apenas a produção de cerveja fraca para não desviar cevada do pão; os alimentos precisavam ser adquiridos por meio de cartões de racionamento — devido à falta de fornecimento de energia elétrica, a feira fechava às 19h.

Somente em 1949 a cerveja de teor alcoólico normal foi novamente autorizada, e naquele mesmo ano a Oktoberfest recuperou seu nome e voltou a ser realizada após uma década de ausência.

Durante aqueles dias de setembro, mais do que os discursos políticos, foram os lederhosen, os dirndls, a gastronomia tradicional e os acordes das bandas folclóricas que ajudaram uma Baviera desmoralizada a começar a cerzir o tecido de sua sociedade.

O ritual do " O'zapft is !" como o conhecemos hoje — aquele do prefeito, do martelo, do grito — foi estabelecido em 1950, quando o então prefeito Thomas Wimmer precisou de 19 golpes para abrir o primeiro barril. Desde então, cada prefeito tenta superar essa marca.

Também desde aquele ano, espera-se o sinal dos canhões para começar a servir o primeiro litro de cerveja em um maßkrug , aquelas enormes canecas de vidro grosso com covinhas que pesam 1,3 quilo vazias e 2,3 quilos cheias.

Quando o festival termina hoje em dia, terão sido cheias entre 6,5 milhões e 7,5 milhões de maßkrug com cervejas produzidas especialmente para o evento pelas únicas seis marcas autorizadas a servir no festival, pois elas são produzidas de acordo com a lei de pureza e dentro dos limites urbanos da cidade de Munique .

A Oktoberfest também criou raízes do outro lado do oceano, pelas mãos de comunidades de imigrantes alemães.

Blumenau, cidade de Santa Catarina fundada em 1850, é conhecida nacionalmente por sua forte herança cultural alemã e por sediar a maior Oktoberfest das Américas.

Mas lá o festival quase não chegou a nascer: estava planejado para 1983, mas uma inundação catastrófica do rio Itajaí-Açu, que devastou a região e deixou 49 mortos, obrigou seu adiamento.

No ano seguinte, quando a cidade se preparava para celebrá-lo, uma segunda enchente voltou a atingi-la.

Ainda assim, as autoridades decidiram seguir em frente: em outubro de 1984 foi realizada a primeira edição, como uma forma deliberada de elevar o ânimo e reativar a economia local.

Foram 102 mil pessoas que brindaram com 103 mil litros de cerveja. Hoje é a segunda maior Oktoberfest do planeta, depois da de Munique .

Um carro de cerveja na Oktoberfest de Blumenau; a cidade foi fundada por Hermann Bruno Otto Blumenau e outros 17 imigrantes alemães. — Foto: Getty Images via BBC

Mas, nas montanhas do estado de Aragua, na Venezuela, há uma versão do festival ainda mais intacta.

Fundada em 1843 por quase 400 colonos vindos da região de Kaiserstuhl — então parte do Grão-Ducado de Baden —, a Colônia Tovar permaneceu praticamente isolada do restante do mundo por um século devido à geografia da região.

Aqui, a herança não é bávara, mas do sudoeste da Alemanha . Seus habitantes ainda preservam a arquitetura enxaimel, a gastronomia da Floresta Negra e, em alguns casos, o alemão coloniero, um dialeto alemânico único no mundo.

Realizada desde o fim dos anos 1970, a Oktoberfest da cidade se destaca pela preservação das tradições, com cervejas artesanais que dão continuidade ao legado da família Benitz, responsável por instalar ali a primeira cervejaria do país em meados do século 19.

Enquanto isso, no sul do Chile, a tradição cervejeira está ligada à história do próprio Estado. Em 1845, o governo promulgou a Lei de Imigração Seletiva com o objetivo de povoar e desenvolver economicamente as terras austrais.

Milhares de famílias alemãs se estabeleceram na região do lago Llanquihue e, em 1984, seus descendentes organizaram a primeira Bierfest de Llanquihue no Clube Ginástico Alemão da cidade para preservar seus costumes.

Diferentemente das feiras comerciais modernas, o evento mantém um forte caráter familiar e comunitário. As receitas tradicionais de salsichas e confeitaria ( Kuchen ) são preparadas pelos tataranetos daqueles pioneiros agrícolas.

Do outro lado da Cordilheira dos Andes, em uma cidade de Córdoba fundada nos anos 1930 por imigrantes alpinos, a festa da cerveja já era realizada havia quase duas décadas.

Em 1957, os moradores de Villa General Belgrano, na Argentina, depois de um grande esforço comunitário, finalmente conseguiram pavimentar a rua principal. Para comemorar, organizaram uma festa com uma orquestra e compartilharam um barril de cerveja na praça central.

A festa fez tanto sucesso que foi repetida e, desde 1963, é realizada ininterruptamente todo mês de outubro como a Festa Nacional da Cerveja.

Além da música centro-europeia e dos trajes tiroleses, o festival inclui, entre outras atrações curiosas, uma singular procissão de cães da raça dachshund.

articles.title: Day after Thar-cab road rage in Gurgaon, fresh car-ramming video surfaces
articles.summary: GURGAON: A day after a video showing a Thar repeatedly ramming into a cab in Sector 89 went viral on social media, another video of a similar road rag.
articles.body: GURGAON: A day after a video showing a Thar repeatedly ramming into a cab in Sector 89 went viral on social media, another video of a similar road rage incident surfaced on Saturday, this time from Sector 38, where two car drivers allegedly rammed their vehicles into each other following an altercation.The video, which has been circulating on social media, shows a Maruti Baleno and a Hyundai Aura repeatedly hitting each other on a road late at night.At one point, a man is also seen being struck by one of the vehicles. The car then appears to move towards him again, in what seems to be an attempt to run him over, before he narrowly moves out of its path.Police, however, said no complaint had been received in connection with the incident and no FIR had been registered as of Saturday evening.“We have not received any complaint regarding the matter. Therefore, no FIR has been registered,” a police officer said.The circumstances leading to the altercation, the identities of those involved and whether anyone was injured are yet to be established.Police are also expected to verify the video and ascertain the sequence of events if a complaint is submitted.The incident comes a day after a similar case in Sector 89, where four men travelling in a Delhi-registered Thar allegedly got into a fight before one of them repeatedly rammed the SUV into a Rapido cab.Police said the four men had an argument inside the Thar, which turned physical.Two of them then booked a Rapido cab to leave the spot. As they were getting into the cab, the Thar driver allegedly drove towards it and rammed it.He then reversed the SUV, accelerated and struck the cab several times.The impact deployed both front airbags of the cab and caused extensive damage to its front and side. articles.title: US fears rapid escalation in Mideast after Houthis attack Riyadh
articles.summary: The United States warned Saturday that hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthis could "escalate rapidly" after a missile attack targeted Riya...
articles.body:
The United States warned Saturday that hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthis could "escalate rapidly" after a missile attack targeted Riyadh for the first time since the Yemen conflict resumed.

US President Donald Trump cut short a weekend at Camp David, a secluded presidential complex in rural Maryland, to return unexpectedly to the White House on Saturday.

The White House gave no explanation for the early return, which comes as a new threshold was crossed in the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, who control a large part of Yemen and are fighting government forces backed by a coalition led by Riyadh.

Loud explosions rang out twice on Saturday in the Saudi capital, where AFP journalists saw a fuel tank bearing the logo of oil giant Aramco on fire near the airport.

"This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly," the US State Department warned, adding American citizens outside the Middle East should "seriously reconsider travel to and through the region".

The Houthis's lightning offensive seizing swathes of Yemeni territory in recent weeks has left hundreds dead and, according to the UN, displaced more than 110,000 people.

These clashes and the subsequent hostilities with the kingdom have already disrupted Saudi Arabia's exports -- the world's leading supplier of crude oil -- as well as maritime traffic.

The Riyadh-led coalition confirmed Saturday evening on X that a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards the capital was "successfully intercepted and destroyed".

The coalition added that the pro-Iranian fighters had tried to target "civilians and civilian infrastructure" in several cities in the west of the kingdom, including the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, an important export hub for Saudi oil.

It said these attacks were "thwarted by the Gulf monarchy's air defences".

Saudi Arabia has responded with scores of airstrikes on Houthi-held areas but failed to stop the advance.

The Houthis said it had responded to recent Saudi attacks by carrying out "two successful military operations using a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones", Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement on Telegram.

"The first targeted sensitive sites in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and the second targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu."

Saudi authorities had earlier issued an overnight air raid alert.

Hours after the early morning alert, residents told AFP on condition of anonymity that they heard what sounded like a round of explosions echoing through parts of the Saudi capital.

This is the first time since Yemen's civil war resumed that strikes have threatened the Saudi capital, piling further pressure on a global economy already rocked by seven months of war between the US and Iran.

"The area is under a hostile aerial threat," according to a message received just before 3:00 am by Riyadh residents, urging them to stay indoors.

AFP journalists then heard two explosions, before the Saudi civil defence agency lifted the alert half an hour later.

"I heard the alarm, then my windows shook," a Riyadh resident told AFP. Another resident described the attack as "terrifying".

The incident comes days after Riyadh accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca on Wednesday, denouncing it as a "cowardly terrorist attack" on Islam's holy city, which welcomes millions of pilgrims each year. The Houthis strongly denied the accusation, calling it a "worn-out lie".

The group has reported scores of retaliatory strikes carried out daily by Riyadh since their offensive this month to take over the country's entire Red Sea coast, giving them control over the vital Bab al-Mandab strait.

The United States, according to US news platform Axios, last week refused a Saudi request to strike the Houthis.

Washington approved a $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to the kingdom on Thursday to help Riyadh "deter current and future threats", the US State Department said.

War in Yemen broke out in 2014 when the Houthis seized control of the capital Sanaa and other regions, triggering a military intervention led by Saudi Arabia in March 2015.

The fragile truce reached in 2022 between the warring parties collapsed in July, when the Houthis defied Riyadh's control of Yemeni airspace by allowing an Iranian aircraft to land in Yemen.

The apparent attack came as the Houthis improve their defences in newly conquered territory along Yemen's Red Sea coastline, with members of the group telling AFP they have been installing radar and digging tunnels.

articles.title: State funeral honours Hong Kong’s first post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa
articles.summary: Selected by Beijing in 1996, Tung Chee-hwa’s tenure shaped post-colonial Hong Kong during a turbulent political era.
articles.body:
Hong Kong has given a state funeral to Tung Chee-hwa, its first post-colonial leader, only the third time the city has granted such an honour since Britain returned it to Chinese rule in 1997.

Senior Chinese and Hong Kong officials bid farewell to Tung at the Hong Kong Funeral Home in North Point on Sunday, a day after a public vigil that drew dozens of political and business figures.

Tung, Hong Kong’s first chief executive, died on September 8 at the age of 89.

Members of the public could pay their respects by signing condolence books at three community halls until Sunday noon.

The funeral committee, made up of 87 members, was chaired by Shi Taifeng, a senior Chinese Communist Party Politburo member and vice chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), the top political advisory body, underlining the level of official backing from Beijing.

Shi attended the funeral alongside Xia Baolong, Beijing’s top official for Hong Kong and Macau affairs; current chief executive John Lee; former chief executives Leung Chun-ying, Carrie Lam and Donald Tsang; and other political and business figures, reported government-funded Radio Television Hong Kong (RTHK).

Lee and Leung were among the pallbearers who carried Tung’s coffin, draped in China’s national flag, from the hall to a hearse, which headed to Cape Collinson Crematorium.

A shipping tycoon with little political experience, Tung was selected in 1996 by a Beijing-appointed committee to become Hong Kong’s first leader after the 1997 handover from Britain.

Tung led the city through the 1997 Asian financial crisis and the 2003 SARS outbreak, and mass protests that year forced him to shelve proposed national security legislation.

He was re-elected unopposed in 2002 but resigned in 2005, midway through his second term, citing poor health, in a move widely seen as driven by Beijing’s loss of confidence in him.

He went on to serve as a vice chairman of the CPPCC until 2023.

Two business leaders, industrialist Ann Tse-kai and tycoon Henry Fok, who both served as vice chairs of the CPPCC, were given state funerals in 2000 and 2006, respectively.

Chinese state media described Tung as a “renowned patriot”, while his successor, Tsang, called him “an easy-going, gentle and refined man with a broad-minded outlook and far-reaching vision”.

Critics recalled his tenure as marked by governance struggles and public discontent that never fully recovered after the financial crisis.

articles.title: Earl Spencer tells BBC Harry and Meghan's media treatment echoes what happened to Diana
articles.summary: Princess Diana's brother describes press coverage of Prince Harry and Meghan as a "cancerous influence in their life" and says he saw his sister cry "tears of despair" over interest in her.
articles.body:
Earl Spencer has told the BBC the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's treatment at the hands of the media has "echoes" of what happened to his sister Diana, Princess of Wales.

He described press coverage of Prince Harry and Meghan as a "cancerous influence in their life" and said it would be "beholden on people to learn from Diana's example".

The Sussexes, who recently returned to the UK from California six years after stepping back from royal duties, have been repeatedly critical of the media.

It comes after the BBC reported on Friday how Earl Spencer says he was "telling the truth" when he claimed King Charles said people would forget Diana "soon enough" in a phone call in the days after her death .

Bitter row over Diana book brings back unhappy times for royals

'I'm telling the truth': Earl Spencer defends Diana book claims about Charles in BBC interview

Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg at his Althorp estate, Earl Spencer was asked if he believed Diana would "identify" with the scrutiny the Duke and Duchess of Sussex face.

"If you look at an article in a tabloid about Diana or the couple that you were mentioning, Harry and Meghan, you know, they can be really, really unpleasant," he replied.

"And I think it would be really beholden on people to learn from Diana's example.

"I'm not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who's being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life."

He said he saw Diana's "tears of despair" when describing the impact of media coverage on her, adding she was "very, very sensitive to criticism".

Earl Spencer said his sister - who married the then-Prince Charles in 1981 - was "really brought low by all that criticism", describing it as a "pity" to see "echoes of that now" in the treatment of his nephew Prince Harry and wife Meghan.

He also said he thought there was a media perception that he was "on Harry's side" but insisted: "I'm on my deceased sister's sons' side, both of them and if either of them wanted anything, then I'd be equally there for them."

Princess Diana was subject to huge press interest right up until her death in a car crash in Paris on 31 August 1997.

In the eulogy he delivered at her funeral, Earl Spencer accused the media of being on a "permanent quest...to bring her down" and said newspapers had been threatened by her "genuine goodness".

His comments about the Sussexes come just weeks after the pair returned to the UK.

They have long been critical of their treatment by the British press as well as the support they received from the Royal Family prior to their decision to leave the UK.

Speaking in the couple's 2021 interview with Oprah Winfrey, Prince Harry accused the tabloid media of having created a "toxic environment" of "control and fear".

Meghan, meanwhile, said in the couple's 2022 Netflix series that "no matter how hard I tried, no matter how good I was, no matter what I did, they [the media] were still going to find a way to destroy me".

In July this year, Prince Harry and six others including Liz Hurley and Sir Elton John lost a privacy case against the publisher of the Daily Mail, and may face a legal bill of up to £34.5m.

In separate, earlier legal battles, the Duke of Sussex beat the Mirror Group in court, and the News Group out of court, forcing a settlement, damages, payout and apology.

Earl Spencer's interview with the BBC was his first since the Palace issued a strongly-worded response to his claims about King Charles.

That statement said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

Earl Spencer, in comments first reported on Friday, reacted to it by saying: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"

He added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life.

"I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."

Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous".

In his response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."

When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."

Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family.

In further extracts published on Thursday, he claimed how the King "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after Diana's death, alleging Charles sounded like a "lottery winner".

articles.title: Why do people want to see Norfolk's police commissioner on stage?
articles.summary: What led to Colin Sutton becoming a box office draw who could tour more than 100 theatres
articles.body:
A £79,000 a year police commissioner has been under fire for plans to carry out a 127-date stage show tour.

Opposition parties questioned how Reform UK's Colin Sutton, could focus on his job overseeing Norfolk Constabulary while travelling across the UK.

Eventually, Sutton dropped out of the "ridiculous" theatre run following a backlash.

But this would have been his sequel to a tour that saw him appear at more than a hundred venues. So why is he such a box-office draw?

Most voters do not know who their commissioner is – the government says that fewer than 20% of people could name them.

But Sutton is not a typical police commissioner.

Following a decades-long career in policing, Sutton has been described as "one of the UK's greatest living detectives" by the promoters of his show.

Born in 1960, he joined the Metropolitan Police in the early 1980s.

He worked his way up the ranks in different forces, but it was his role back in the Met as detective chief inspector which saw him thrust into the public spotlight.

In 2004 he led the investigation to catch serial killer Levi Bellfield , who had murdered Milly Dowler, Marsha McDonnell and Amelie Delagrange.

He also oversaw the latter stages of the long-running investigation to capture Night Stalker rapist Delroy Grant .

Sutton retired in 2011 as one of the UK's most high-profile officers.

What did he do after leaving the police?

In 2019 he released his first book, Manhunt, detailing the investigation into Bellfield's capture.

This was later adapted into a three-part ITV drama starring Martin Clunes as Sutton.

A follow-up book and TV series were released in 2021, and Sutton also became a regular media commentator on policing issues.

Meanwhile, he began featuring in documentaries looking at the major cases he had been involved in.

Alongside his TV and writing work, Sutton started presenting live shows in person, including one in Norwich back in 2022.

With the true-crime genre continuing to grow in popularity, there was demand from audiences to hear Sutton talking about his experiences in policing.

That led to him embarking on a long-running stage tour, "Makings of a Murderer", in 2024 and 2025, performing at more than 100 venues.

It was such a success that the promotion company, Entertainers, planned a sequel show to run across 127 dates next year.

The job of Norfolk Police and Crime Commissioner (PCC) became vacant in June, when Sarah Taylor announced she was immediately quitting .

Despite the government planning to scrap the role in two years, saying it is not needed. a by-election was called.

Sutton comfortably won the job of overseeing the local force and the £79,000 salary that comes with it.

But then earlier this month, plans were revealed for an 11-month tour for 2027, with a teaser video on YouTube featuring Sutton announcing "I'm back".

He faced immediate criticism, with political rivals such as Liberal Democrat Steff Aquarone pointing out that he was performing a similar number of dates as Taylor Swift would do on a tour.

Following growing pressure, Sutton announced on Wednesday said he was pulling out, calling the number of dates "ridiculous".

He later told the BBC he was trying to help Entertainers find a "suitable substitute" to replace him.

"The tour will go ahead, but I will not be appearing in it," he said.

articles.title: Germany’s Berlin, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania states head to polls
articles.summary: About 3.8 million people in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania are eligible to vote on Sunday.
articles.body:
Voters in the eastern German states of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania are heading to the polls as far-right and far-left gains threaten to affect the political standing of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

About 2.5 million people are eligible to vote in the city-state of Berlin, Germany’s capital, and nearly 1.3 million in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday. Polling booths in both states – traditionally seen as left-leaning – opened at 8am local time (06:00 GMT) and will close at 6pm (16:00 GMT).

Pressure on Merz has been mounting after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) delivered a major defeat to his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party two weeks ago in the key state of Saxony-Anhalt . The AfD fell just short of an absolute majority, which would have allowed it to govern on its own.

After just 16 months in power, Merz’s approval ratings have plunged to about 14 percent, the latest polls suggest, as he struggles to push through promised economic and social welfare reforms with his centre-left coalition partners, the Social Democratic Party (SPD), raising doubts among fellow party members about whether he can continue to lead.

In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the CDU is an onlooker to the main battle between the SPD’s popular state premier Manuela Schwesig and the AfD’s lead candidate, former radio presenter Leif-Erik Holm.

While the AfD was polling at 36 percent against the SPD’s 37 percent, Merz’s CDU, at just 6 percent, was dangerously close to the 5 percent hurdle needed to stay in the state parliament, according to public broadcaster ZDF.

Reporting from a polling station in Schwerin, Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane said there was “very much all to play for” in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

“The race between the AfD here and the Social Democrat government is very close indeed,” he added, pointing out the recent opinion polls.

In Berlin, the CDU is running a tight race against the far-left Die Linke (The Left), which promises drastic measures to solve a dire housing crisis and is popular with young people.

Regional elections would not usually draw much interest outside Germany, but the AfD’s success in Saxony-Anhalt, which it sees as the first step towards winning federal elections due in 2029, has sent shockwaves through Europe.

“Saxony-Anhalt was certainly a revolution for the German party system,” Florian Hartleb, a professor of international relations at Modul University in Vienna and expert on far-right movements, told Al Jazeera.

Hartleb said the AfD had been “fundamentally excluded” from the power system, with the other political parties trying “everything” against it in recent years. “But it didn’t work out,” he said, citing voters’ dissatisfaction over migration, the economy and social inequality.

Merz has reportedly scheduled a crisis CDU meeting and cleared his calendar to deal with potential aftershocks from Sunday’s elections.

articles.title: Reform Wales' chaotic week - An arrest, defection and new leader
articles.summary: How an extraordinary seven days that rocked the party unfolded.
articles.body:
"It's been challenging but we've come through it," said Reform's chief whip in the Senedd, Llŷr Powell, as he reflected on the past seven days.

The week began with the party's leader in Wales being arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.

Dan Thomas said he had been "released without charge" and had "done nothing wrong".

Confirmation of his arrest was swiftly followed by news of a Reform Senedd member's defection to Plaid Cymru.

This is the story of how that "challenging" week unfolded.

Politician who switched from Reform to Plaid 'lied about her beliefs', says Richard Tice

Last Sunday morning, Thomas was at the BBC's offices in Cardiff to appear as a guest on the Politics Wales programme.

Later that day, he was arrested before being released on bail.

Journalists got wind of the arrest on Monday evening, which is also when senior Reform figures in Wales began to find out.

A few people at Reform HQ in London, including Nigel Farage, had already been told.

On Tuesday morning, Reform Members of the Senedd (MSs) gathered for their weekly group meeting.

With the "rumour mill going wild" there was "confusion" within the group.

Dan Thomas was not present, and the MSs were not given the full picture, but they were warned that the party faced "a tough few days".

It was soon announced that Thomas would not take his usual spot in the chamber for First Minister's Questions and would be replaced by his deputy, Helen Jenner.

At that point Reform said his absence was due to "personal reasons".

But as time went on it became clear that the story was about to break.

A legal letter sent to media organisations by a Reform barrister would not be enough to block the reporting of Thomas's arrest.

BBC Wales and others had secured confirmation that Thomas had been arrested and so the party needed to act.

That's when Thomas sent a WhatsApp message to his party's MSs explaining the situation. Some of them were in the chamber at the time.

In his media statement Thomas said he was standing down as leader.

He remains a Reform MS for Casnewydd Islwyn.

Then came the next bombshell as it emerged that Reform MS for Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg Sarah Cooper-Lesadd was defecting to Plaid Cymru.

Reform only found out about it after BBC Wales asked the party for a response to the story.

Moments earlier she had been sitting on the Reform benches and had been due to speak for the party in the chamber.

Most of Plaid Cymru's MSs - including some government ministers - were only told about the defection plan at their group meeting earlier in the day.

The defection needed the group's approval and some Plaid MSs wanted assurances that Cooper-Lesadd fully understood what it meant to be a Plaid Cymru member.

The defection was approved with the necessary two thirds majority. But it wasn't backed by everyone.

At a hastily arranged news conference in the Senedd, Cooper-Lesadd said her switch to Plaid followed "a period of reflection and deliberation" and that she had found "the right political home".

The move was completely unconnected to Dan Thomas's arrest.

Neither Cooper-Lesadd nor Plaid will say how or when the talks over the defection began, only that the process had gone on for "a while" and she had been on a "journey".

The defection, just four months on from May's Senedd election, has raised fresh questions about the electoral process where voters were required to back a party rather than an individual.

Jess Blair, from the Electoral Reform Society, said that while defections were "nothing new" there was more of an "accountability gap" given the Welsh voting system.

"When this electoral system was put in place a review mechanism was also built into that process and what we need now is to really see that review take place," she said.

By Wednesday, Reform's focus was on appointing a new leader.

A party official from London came to explain the process to MSs, and Dan Thomas was also at that meeting.

As is the case when a new leader is needed, various names were being discussed.

James Evans was seen as one obvious contender.

When it was announced that he would make a media statement reporters scrambled to hear what he had to say.

"Having consulted with my family...I will not be putting my name forward," he said, despite "a majority" of the party's MSs backing him to take over.

By Thursday morning it was looking increasingly likely that Helen Jenner would be the next leader.

While Reform UK bosses in London have not had any formal input to the process, sources say there have been "signals" that Jenner - a Farage ally since the UKIP days - would be seen as a good choice in HQ.

Confirmation of Jenner's appointment is expected as soon as Monday.

"I feel we're more united than ever," said Llŷr Powell.

"For us it's a new start next week and that's what we're building on."

articles.title: Jaguar Land Rover suppliers call for shift to aerospace
articles.summary: Suppliers tell the government that Britain's manufacturing future lies beyond car production.
articles.body:
Major Jaguar Land Rover suppliers have urged the government to help automotive manufacturers move into aerospace and defence, warning that large-scale car production in the UK faces long-term decline.

In an open letter to the prime minister, chancellor and West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker, industry leaders argued Britain's automotive supply chain was "not in decline" but "in the wrong market".

The intervention comes nearly a fortnight after JLR announced plans to cut 4,000 jobs.

The Treasury said it recognised the uncertainty facing workers and was supporting the automotive sector through grants, lower energy costs and investment in electric vehicle production.

JLR has its global headquarters in Coventry and plants in Solihull, Wolverhampton and Halewood.

Signatories to the letter said the redundancies were "the first visible crack" in a UK automotive supply chain supporting about 183,000 manufacturing jobs.

The group, which includes Coventry-based Evtec, Solihull-based Artifex and the Confederation of British Metal Forming, said suppliers faced rising energy costs, growing overseas competition and increasing pressure from vehicle manufacturers sourcing components abroad.

David Roberts, chairman of Evtec, said manufacturers believed high-volume car production in the UK was entering a decade of decline.

Speaking on BBC Politics Midlands, he said: "We want to take action today rather than wait for that to happen."

Roberts argued there was a "very big opportunity" for manufacturers to redirect skills, factories and investment into the UK's expanding aerospace and defence sectors.

The letter said automotive suppliers already possessed many of the capabilities needed to support aircraft, defence equipment and military vehicles, but warned firms needed help to make the transition.

"The capacity exists. The people exist. What is missing is the bridge," it said.

The manufacturers called for lower industrial energy costs, support to help firms qualify for aerospace and defence contracts, and a West Midlands programme to accelerate the shift into those sectors.

The letter was signed by executives representing businesses with more than 8,600 direct employees, alongside the Confederation of British Metal Forming, which represents about 75,000 workers.

According to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, Chinese-owned brands accounted for about 15% of new car registrations in the UK in 2025 and 2026.

The suppliers argued that competitors overseas benefited from lower energy costs, greater automation and, in some cases, government subsidies.

A Treasury spokesperson said Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds had met JLR and trade union representatives following the redundancy announcement and pointed to government backing for electric vehicle production through the £2.5bn DRIVE35 programme.

The government said manufacturers were also expected to benefit from measures to reduce industrial electricity costs and support investment in the sector.

articles.title: Bridgewater Hall: 30th anniversary concert and Hallé performance
articles.summary: One of Manchester's best-loved venues marks its 30th anniversary with a season of special concerts.
articles.body:
One of Manchester's best-known cultural venues, Bridgewater Hall, is marking its 30th anniversary with a season of special concerts.

The first will take place later and aim to blend sounds from the city's rich and diverse musical history with performances from Rowetta, Matt Wilde and the Greater Manchester Youth Orchestra.

The Hallé Orchestra, based at Bridgewater Hall for its entire history, will pay homage to its 1996 opening night concert with a commemorative performance on Thursday.

Bridgewater Hall's CEO Andrew Bolt said the concerts would reflect the "evolving landscape" of Manchester's musical history, tying together its classical heritage with more contemporary performances.

A new episode of the BBC Sounds series Hidden Manchester explores how the venue represents the city's history with classical music.

Bolt explained that the Hallé had played a particularly important role in the hall's origin.

"When it was decided that a new home (for the Hallé) was something important to put together, the building was constructed as part of an urban redevelopment project," he said.

"We're delighted to have such a close relationship. We look forward to another 30 years!"

Musicologist Stacy Jarvis has studied Manchester's musical history.

She said artists had been travelling to the city to perform since as early as the 1820s.

"It was like Oasis today - they had to perform here," explained Jarvis.

"Every band that we know today has to perform in Manchester. It was a must."

She said Manchester's music was just as important to its history as its famous industrial past.

"Manchester's extraordinary industrial growth created the wealth and population that helped its musical culture flourish," she said.

"Manchester was deciding what kind of cultural city it wanted to be.

"Bridgewater Hall became a part of that identity."

Bolt described the hall as "one of the most important" classical music venues in the country.

"It has really embedded itself into the cultural landscape of Manchester itself," he added. "It's so loved, and it's recognised as such a fabulous place to perform or come and see a performance."

"We're looking to continue that legacy - and grow it. It's all about relevance, both in the classical and contemporary musical spheres."

articles.title: Bid to remember Force 135 leader behind Channel Island liberation
articles.summary: Brig Snow was the senior British officer responsible for liberating the Channel Islands in 1945.
articles.body:
A campaign to help remember a "significant World War Two commander" is under way after his final resting place was discovered earlier this year.

Brig Alfred Snow was the senior British officer responsible for the liberation of the Channel Islands in 1945 after five years of Nazi rule.

The location of his final resting place remained unknown until earlier this summer , when it was discovered his ashes had been scattered in Taunton, Somerset.

The British Channel Islands WWII Remembrance Campaign said it was now fundraising to create "appropriate remembrance in Somerset".

Campaign leader Kev South said a public fundraising appeal, events, tour and dedicated website would form part of a "co-ordinated national campaign to ensure his place in British and Channel Islands history is finally recognised".

It comes after the Bailiff of Jersey and the Bailiff of Guernsey agreed Brigadier Snow should receive "appropriate remembrance" .

He commanded Force 135, the British and Commonwealth formation of about 6,000 tasked with liberating the islands after almost five years of German occupation, in Operation Nestegg - the planned peaceful liberation of the islands.

After inquiries with Somerset Council and Taunton Crematorium, the remembrance campaign group learned his ashes were scattered within the town's Garden of Rest.

The group discovered he died in 1983 at the age of 85.

A spokesperson for Somerset Council, which manages the crematorium, previously said no memorials were allowed on the lawn.

articles.title: Bristol nipple tattooist frustrated by social media censorship
articles.summary: Lauren Carter says her tattoos on post-mastectomy patients are flagged as nudity and banned.
articles.body:
A medical tattoo artist has described the online censorship of nipple tattoos for mastectomy patients as "wholly unfair and discriminatory".

Lauren Carter, based in Hanham near Bristol, says social media bots and algorithms often mistakenly flag her hyper-realistic work as "inappropriate nudity".

Carter has been banned from posting numerous times, and her pictures have been permanently removed, which she says leaves her "struggling" to reach new clients.

A spokesperson for Facebook and Instagram owner Meta said it "continues to work on improving" how it identifies and protects medical and health-related content.

'Helping people with music is my mission'

Mother expected to plead guilty over child deaths

Because medical tattoos are designed to look as realistic as possible, social media bots and algorithms can sometimes confuse the inked 3D-effect for bare skin.

A Meta spokesperson confirmed post-mastectomy scarring and areola tattoos are allowed on Facebook and Instagram, but its systems "occasionally make mistakes".

"We understand how frustrating that can be, which is why we allow users to appeal these decisions and we continue to work on improving how we identify and protect medical and health-related content," they said.

"We recognise the important role medical tattooists play in supporting breast cancer survivors, and we want this content on our platforms."

Despite posting disclaimers and covering the nipple tattoo with emojis, Carter says each update to her online portfolio jeopardises years of hard work and positive reviews.

"It really does upset me - there's a sense of injustice," she said.

"I'm annoyed and frustrated, not only for myself, but for the people who are looking for this sort of thing and can't find it. I don't know how else to reach people."

Carter says her posts are automatically removed "nine times out of 10". She always appeals the decision, but "it's as if nobody even reads it".

"It's interesting how the photos I post of male nipples following my treatments do not get banned or reported as a sexual image," she added.

"For me, this work is about so much more than beauty. It is about helping people feel confident, comfortable and like themselves again."

Jessica Bowler, a nurse from Bristol, underwent a double mastectomy with implant reconstruction at the age of 32 following a breast cancer diagnosis in 2019.

"Although I knew the treatment was necessary to save my life, it was still incredibly difficult physically and emotionally," she said.

"I would look in the mirror and almost not recognise myself. My chest was a reminder of everything I had been through."

Bowler said the decision to get areola reconstruction tattoos marked an important milestone in her recovery, describing the procedure as "empowering".

"The tattoos weren't about vanity; they were about feeling comfortable in my own skin," she said.

"It's difficult to explain unless you've been through it, but having something restored that cancer took away can be incredibly powerful."

The 39-year-old described the online censoring of nipple tattoos as "really upsetting", as it prevents survivors from exploring the options available to them post-surgery.

"They shouldn't be treated as something shameful or sexual," she said.

"[People] who've been through breast cancer should be able to share their stories and help each other without being censored."

articles.title: This private island home in US' Maine costs $450,000 - but there's a catch
articles.summary: News News: A tree-lined private island on Maine's largest lake is on the market for $450,000, offering buyers a renovated cabin, waterfront views and plenty of p.
articles.body: A tree-lined private island on Maine's largest lake is on the market for $450,000, offering buyers a renovated cabin, waterfront views and plenty of privacy, but there's one unusual catch.The roughly 0.1-acre island on Moosehead Lake was listed earlier this month. It features a one-bedroom, one-bathroom cabin renovated in 2022 and about 200 feet of waterfront, according to property listings.The home is surrounded by the lake and accessible from the mainland by boat or snowmobile, depending on the season. But despite its idyllic setting, the property does not have a conventional drinking-water.The property uses a lake-drawn water system, with water pumped directly from Moosehead Lake into the home's plumbing. The water can be used for cooking and showering but is not considered safe for drinking, Realtor Nicole Hilton told the Daily Mail.The property also has no septic system, meaning the new owner will have to use a composting toilet and bring drinking water to the island.Despite those limitations, Hilton said the cabin could appeal to buyers looking for a low-maintenance second home. “I see a lot of people now looking for modern camps with no maintenance, and this doesn't require much maintenance, because it's all brand new,” Hilton said.“It pretty much is zero maintenance, so I think that is what a lot of people would like about it,” Hilton added.Inside the $450,000 houseInside, the cabin has an open-plan living area with warm wood finishes, large windows overlooking the lake and a stone accent wall centred around a wood-burning stove, according to the New York Post.The adjoining kitchen features wood cabinetry, open shelving, stainless-steel appliances and its own island. The bathroom has also been renovated, with a glass-enclosed walk-in shower, tiled walls and a pebble-stone floor inspired by the surrounding landscape.The cabin is insulated and has generator power, lake-drawn water and both Rinnai and wood heating. The property would likely appeal to a couple looking for a private waterfront second home rather than someone seeking a conventional full-time residence.The island offers views of Moosehead Lake's blue-green waters and is near Lily Bay State Park, where visitors can moor boats and explore the surrounding area. Although the area attracts tourists during the summer, Hilton said the island itself remains relatively quiet.“It's certainly quiet where it's located,” Hilton told the Daily Mail. “The lake is 40 miles long, so it's huge. You're not going to see a ton of boating activity go by.”The closest town is Greenville, about a 20-minute drive from the mainland access point, where residents can shop for groceries and visit restaurants. The property is nearly three hours north of Portland, about 90 minutes from Bangor and roughly an hour from the Canadian border.The island's location also means access requires some planning. articles.title: Two killed in Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow, says Russia
articles.summary: Moscow mayor says Russia has intercepted 1,600 drones since Saturday, including 450 directed at the capital.
articles.body:
At least two people have been killed and a major refinery damaged in a Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, including the capital city, as the Russian parliamentary elections enter their final day.

Moscow’s Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Sunday more than 1,600 drones had been intercepted, 450 of which were heading for the capital.

Meanwhile, in Ukraine, authorities said at least four people were killed in overnight Russian attacks on the Kyiv region, including three children.

The attacks come as Russia and Ukraine continue to escalate long-range strikes against each other.

Moscow regional Governor Andrey Vorobyov said on social media that a 44-year-old woman and an elderly man were killed in two separate Ukrainian attacks. A fire triggered by a drone crashing into a 21-storey building forced the evacuation of 400 people, Vorobyov said.

Sobyanin said a facility at the Moscow oil refinery was also damaged in the wave of attacks, and emergency services were on the scene. The major refinery has already been hit by Ukrainian strikes in recent months.

He accused Ukraine of attempting to interfere with Russia’s tightly controlled three-day election.

“The unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed,” he said on Telegram.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy praised the strikes, saying: “Our long-range responses had a very significant impact in the Moscow region last night.”

“One of Russia’s key oil industry facilities and the aggressor’s logistics facility were hit. These are billions of dollars that sustain the war machine,” he posted on X.

Separately, the head ⁠of ⁠Russia’s Central Election Commission said ⁠a drone attack on ⁠a civilian bus killed two people, including an election official, ‌in a Russian-occupied part of Kherson region in Ukraine, the RIA Novosti news agency reported.

The strikes come as Kyiv has intensified its long-range drone campaign against Russia, particularly targeting energy infrastructure to cut off a vital source of Kremlin revenue used to fund its war effort, now in its fifth year.

Al Jazeera’s Dmitry Medvedenko, reporting from Moscow, said this was among the largest single-day attacks on Russia since the war began.

“I have not seen numbers this large in the four and a half years of this conflict, especially in the past six months when Ukrainian attacks have escalated,” he said.

Medvedenko said it is no coincidence that this large-scale attack is happening on the last day of the Russian elections.

“This is the most important final day of the election. Will it cause people to express their frustration with how this conflict has been affecting them directly after four and a half years? Will it cause them to rally around the flag here, show unity, as President Vladimir Putin was calling on people to do? We will have to wait and see.”

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s air force reported that Russia launched 138 drones of various types across the country overnight, according to the Interfax-Ukraine news agency. It said air defences managed to shoot down 101 of them.

A woman and her two three-year-old children died when a Russian drone hit a home in the Kyiv region, according to the emergency service. Kyiv region’s Governor Tymur Tkachenko said a girl died in hospital after a separate drone strike in another district.

Tkachenko said the region endured more than a day of attacks, with 31 sites damaged across five districts. The southwestern Fastiv district sustained the most damage, with 24 sites hit, including homes, industrial and utility buildings, vehicles, and the grounds of an agricultural enterprise.

Russia has been repeatedly attacking Kyiv and the surrounding region with drones in recent weeks.

Reporting from Kyiv, Al Jazeera’s Rory Challands said the Kyiv region has been targeted frequently in recent days.

“These strikes have been going on in Kyiv, where you get the air raid sirens going off pretty much around the clock, with drones coming in and missiles being used on occasion as well. So, it’s part of the reality of life in Ukraine at the moment.”

articles.title: Trump’s sanctions, inflation and a collapsing economy leaves Iran’s sick exposed
articles.summary: When 35-year-old Sima walked into a Tehran pharmacy, her eyes raced across the shelves behind the counter, searching for the box that would keep her kidneys from failing. Without it, she was running out of time.
articles.body: When 35-year-old Sima walked into a Tehran pharmacy, her eyes raced across the shelves behind the counter, searching for the box that would keep her kidneys from failing. Without it, she was running out of time. She finally found the medication in the seventh pharmacy she visited, in a wealthy Tehran neighborhood. Her relief faded when the pharmacist told her that the price had once again gone up, leaving her with no choice but to underdose the lifesaving medication. As US sanctions suffocate Iran’s economy, ordinary people with chronic conditions and serious illnesses are struggling to find the medicine they depend on to survive. With severe shortages and daily price increases, many, like Sima, have been forced to cut doses, postpone doctor visits or self-medicate. “They’ve stopped using cancer medication for people who they say are terminal or far along,” said Sima, who did not give CNN her real name so she could speak freely. “They only use it for those who are in the very early stages.” A mother in Tehran who lost her only daughter has been forced to change her antidepressant medication to a less effective locally produced version. Seasonal flu vaccinations have been called off this year after the government failed to procure them from Europe. Cancer patients are selling their televisions and refrigerators to buy overpriced medication. A 55-year-old cancer patient, who asked to remain anonymous, said she, too, is running out of options. “I’ve asked if people who come visit or come back from abroad can bring my medicine back, especially the things we can’t find here or get access, too,” the patient, who lives in Tehran, told CNN. “Between the illness and uncertainty of the war I have a hard time knowing what to do.” Pharmacies in Iran contacted by CNN confirmed shortages and price increases across several categories, including heart medication, which is now offered as a local generic rather than the prescribed brand, cholesterol-lowering pills, which are available but far more expensive, and migraine drugs, which have completely vanished from shop shelves. Iran media reports, however, suggest the shortages are far more wide-reaching, affecting everything from antidepressants to insulin and pregnancy medications. Other drugs are completely unobtainable, leaving Iran’s sick facing astronomically higher prices or a less effective generic version. The shortages have affected almost 800 medications, the head of the Iranian Pharmacists Association Shahram Kalantari told a press conference last month, with pharmacies unable to procure alternatives due to the rising costs. “Everyone says we’re brave,” the cancer patient added in a telephone call. “But I don’t know if being brave means anything when you’re dying.” Mounting debt Iran now manufactures more than 97% of its medicines by volume, Mehdi Pirsalehi, head of the country’s Food and Drug Organization, said in February. Hardest hit are imported specialty drugs that must be paid for in foreign currency. Shortages of these drugs have grown under US President Donald Trump’s maximum-pressure campaign, which has intensified scrutiny of Iran’s banks and impeded exports of oil – the main source of the foreign currency for the Islamic Republic. “This high level of domestic production does not necessarily mean complete self-sufficiency,” said Peivand Bastani, Senior Lecturer at Flinders University and co-author of research examining the effects of sanctions on pharmaceutical procurement in Iran. “Local manufacturing can still depend on imported materials, equipment and technology, while some specialized and high-cost medicines must be imported.” Pharmacies cannot replenish their inventories because insurance companies have stopped paying them, according to Iranian officials. With millions of Iranians covered by insurance, presenting an insured prescription at a pharmacy usually produces nothing, or requires the patient to pay out-of-pocket. Rampant inflation, the collapse of insurance payments, and the government’s inability to sell oil and obtain the foreign currency needed to repay pharmacies have fractured the supply chain. More than 18,000 private pharmacies across the country are now waiting to get paid by insurance companies, officials from Iran’s Pharmacists Association said at a news conference last month, with insurance debts owed to pharmacies reaching almost 800 trillion rials ($300 million) “These pharmacies can no longer afford to continue investing their own capital and then wait a year to receive their outstanding payments,” the head of the association, Shahram Kalantari, said at the time. War destruction US and Israeli airstrikes on Iran earlier this year damaged more than 40 pharmaceutical companies, equipment suppliers and distributors, the spokesman for Iran’s Food and Drug Administration, Mohammad Hashemi, told Iranian state-affiliated media in June. In late March, Israel struck the factory of a major Iranian pharmaceutical company, Tofigh Daru, which produced active ingredients for anticancer drugs and anesthetics. The Israeli military claimed the company provided fentanyl to an Iranian entity conducting “research and development of chemical weapons” - something the company denied. Airstrikes also damaged the historic Pasteur Institute, founded more than a century ago. The Lancet, a medical journal, reported that the attacks had flattened “crucial reference laboratories, including those for genomic surveillance, rabies, HIV/AIDS, viral hepatitis, and vector-borne diseases.” Last month, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that the US would clamp down on the complex network built by Iran over years to allow its entities to evade Washington’s wide-ranging sanctions – a move designed to add pressure on Iran amid a lack of diplomatic resolution. Washington has permitted transactions involving “agricultural commodities, food, medicine, or medical devices to Iran,” but have added some safeguards to ensure such goods are “not diverted by the Iranian regime to fund its nefarious purposes.” In 2019, the US sanctioned Iran’s Central Bank and has since asked foreign governments and institutions seeking protection for payment channels to voluntarily send Washington more information regarding any shipment of medicine to Iran, including details on who is buying it and a written commitment that it will not be resold to a sanctioned individual or entity. Last week, the US administration tightened the rules on other licenses, adopting a “presumed denial” stance on certain licenses and saying applications would be reviewed on a case-by-case basis. Experts say the laborious bureaucratic process has discouraged international firms from doing business with Iran. “Sanctions can obstruct financing and international payments, reduce the willingness of foreign banks and suppliers to engage with Iranian purchasers, and complicate the procurement and importation of medicines, pharmaceutical inputs and manufacturing technology” Bastani of Flinders University said. Although Iran’s leading pharmaceutical firms are not themselves under sanctions, several of the largest are connected to sanctioned charitable conglomerates or to sanctioned individuals. For example, Barkat Pharmaceutical Group, one of the country’s biggest drug makers that led the nation’s vaccine production for Covid-19, is linked to the Execution of Imam Khomeini’s Order, a sanctioned body that answers directly to the Supreme Leader. “Overcompliance” is another issue, said Erich Ferrari, founder of a Washington D.C firm focused on sanctions and enforcement. Banks or trade partners may view a transaction as simply too risky. “Even if you can identify the parties and intermediaries that are not sanctioned, you still have to find banks that are willing to process the transactions and willing to process the trade and take the risk,” Ferrari told CNN. “Banks might say, ‘We don’t really know who’s who in Iran, how the funds will go, where the money is coming from, so let’s just not do the trade.’” Iran was negotiating with the US to unfreeze some funds held in Qatar for humanitarian spending. Those talks have since stalled as Tehran focuses on negotiating the future of the Strait of Hormuz and Washington turns back to diplomacy. “It’s getting harder day by day,” Ferrari said. “I’m actually pretty amazed that Iranians have been able to survive this long given how onerous the sanctions regime is.”

articles.title: Congress calls SIR 'Shah Instigated Removal', flags large-scale voter deletions
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Congress on Sunday took a swipe at Union home minister Amit Shah over the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, alle.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress on Sunday took a swipe at Union home minister Amit Shah over the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, alleging that it was a "Shah Instigated Removal" of voters.Congress general secretary in-charge of communications Jairam Ramesh said the Election Commission began Phase 1 of the SIR process in Bihar in June 2025, followed by Phase 2 in November 2025 across nine states and three Union Territories.According to Jairam Ramesh, 7.8 crore names were deleted during the first two phases, amounting to 13% of the pre-SIR electoral roll.Jairam said Phase 3 began in 16 states and three Union Territories in mid-2026. Citing data from 12 states and two UTs, he claimed that 6.18 crore names had been deleted from a total of 36.06 crore voters."The deletion rate works out to over 17% 2. An additional 5.43 crore voters have been issued notices demanding additional documentation to have their names retained on the electoral roll. The risk of deletion rate works to another 15%. This is an unusually high proportion that reflects structural flaws in the entire SIR process," Jairam said.He questioned how such a large number of voters could still be required to undergo verification after the deletion of millions of names."Thus, a staggering 32% (or about one in three) of voters have had their names deleted or face risk of deletion," Jairam added.He cited Delhi, Chandigarh, Jharkhand, Uttarakhand, Meghalaya, Maharashtra, Telangana, Karnataka, Haryana, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Punjab as states and UTs where he claimed a significant proportion of voters had either been deleted or faced the risk of deletion.The Congress leader also alleged that large-scale deletions were disproportionately affecting voters from economically and socially disadvantaged sections. He further claimed that, in most major states, more women than men had been removed from electoral rolls during the SIR process.Jairam said the exercise had shifted the burden of verification from the state to citizens, who were being asked to produce documents that they may never have been issued. "A test that the overwhelming majority of citizens cannot pass is just a 'machine for exclusion'," he said."SIR is actually a massive Shah Instigated Removal of voters. It is an assault on our Constitution," he added.Tagging his statement on X, he wrote, "SIR is actually a Shah Instigated Removal of voters on a massive scale. Here is a statement on this brazen assault on our Constitution itself."Jairam also said voter lists facing deletion risks had been made publicly available in Karnataka, Telangana and Jharkhand, allowing voters to check their names. He claimed Delhi made its list public only on September 19, 2026, following public pressure, while other BJP-ruled states and Punjab had not done so.The Election Commission has maintained that the SIR, being conducted after 22 years, is aimed at cleaning electoral rolls by removing ineligible and duplicate entries while ensuring that all eligible citizens are included in the rolls.Opposition parties have alleged that the exercise could target voters who do not support the BJP and its allies. The allegations have been rejected by the Election Commission, which has defended the revision as an exercise to ensure accurate and legally eligible electoral rolls.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: West Yorkshire fire chief's funding plea to tackle moor fires
articles.summary: West Yorkshire fire chief Lee Miller says 'any extra resource will help' as the situation worsens.
articles.body:
A senior firefighter has joined calls for more government funding to tackle the growing threat of moor fires.

Lee Miller, a district commander for West Yorkshire Fire & Rescue Service, said this year had been one of the busiest on record.

Crews tackled their first moor fire on Marsden Moor near Huddersfield in April with others appearing across the county throughout the summer, including in Silsden and Baildon near Bradford, and East Ardsley near the M1 in Leeds.

Wildfire incidents across England and Wales topped 1,000 for the second year in a row, according to the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC).

Miller said: "I've been in the service 28 years and dealt with probably handfuls of wildfires in previous years.

"Since 2019 onwards we started to see wildfires occurring in much greater numbers, with larger areas being affected much more frequently due to the climate change."

Miller said the service had adapted using lighter PPE and specialist crews and equipment to tackle wildfires.

He said: "We would welcome any investment into the fire sector and West Yorkshire Fire & Rescue Service to provide extra resource for these types of incidents because our firefighters are extremely stretched.

"As always any extra resource will help as this threat emerges over the next couple of years."

Leeds North West MP Katie White was made climate minister in Prime Minister Andy Burnham's new cabinet.

White is highlighting the need to coordinate efforts to tackle the problem and could lead a wildfire summit on the issue.

She said: "In terms of the land and wildfires, we are looking at how to make sure that we support the land so that there's less likely spread.

"Whether it's around peat or wetting. There are lots of different techniques.

"Then working with our incredible firefighters.

"So that when we do have those fires they have all of the tools necessary to try to curtail the spread of those wildfires."

The National Trust is using re-wetting projects involving sphagnum moss, tree planting and leaky dams as long-term strategies to protect its land.

Others advocate methods of reducing surface vegetation, what they call the fuel load, by controlled burning during the cooler months.

Richard Bailey is from the Peak District Moorland Group which represents 17 grouse shooting estates as well as 50 gamekeepers.

He said: "We need to look at using every tool in the toolkit - which includes re-wetting but it can also include prescribed burns and cutting and grazing.

Most wildfires are caused by human activity, according to the NFCC, whether accidental or deliberate.

The council added: "The impacts of climate change also increases the risk and severity of these incidents."

articles.title: Leaky air traffic control tower at Dumfries museum to be repaired
articles.summary: Visitor safety and displays are being put at risk by water getting into the Dumfries Aviation Museum.
articles.body:
Plans have been lodged to repair a former air traffic control tower in southern Scotland in order to protect the displays at an aviation museum.

They would see replacement doors, roofing and railings put in at the site at Heathhall near Dumfries.

Operators say there is currently a safety risk as, on days when there is wet weather, water is finding its way into displays and also onto floors and stairs creating a slip hazard.

They have submitted plans to Dumfries and Galloway Council to carry out the improvements to the C-listed building in order to let it have a "longer life as the centre piece of the museum".

RAF Dumfries opened in 1940 and was the biggest airfield in south-west Scotland.

It was home to maintenance units and also used as a training base.

After the war it was used for scrapping aircraft and became a training centre for National Service recruits before closing in 1957.

It started a new life in the 1970s following the formation of the Dumfries and Galloway Aviation Group which excavated aircraft wreckage in the area.

Looking for a permanent home to put its artefacts on display it moved onto the Heathhall airfield - initially in the former pilots' flight hut and then in the larger control tower which opened to the public in 1979.

It has grown since then - one of the "jewels in its collection" is a Spitfire which was recovered from Loch Doon in Ayrshire, before being painstakingly put back together.

The operators - all volunteers - are now seeking to carry out work to safeguard the museum control tower's future.

"The air traffic control tower is used to house a number of exhibits," they say in their planning application.

"The current state of the building is that we have water ingress either through the roof or the walls.

"[On] wet weather days water is finding its way into displays but also onto floors and stairs and is a slip hazard."

There are other issues they hope to tackle as well.

"The doors and frames are rotting and will be, if left, a safety hazard as two of the largest doors are now not secured to their frames due to the hinges having fallen off the frame due to the rot of the frame," they added.

"The proposed use is the same as the current use, but with the knowledge that displays will not be ruined, the floors and stairs will be safer and the tower will have a longer life as the centre piece of the museum."
